kind: multi_country_interest
status: approved
buttonLabel: "More about food and wine in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil"
lead: >-
  How can you combine the culinary experiences of Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil in one journey? In Ada Tours' current 20-day itinerary through six countries, the main confirmed food-and-wine stop among these three is Buenos Aires: a tango show with dinner, traditional dishes and Argentine wines. The Brazilian days take place in Rio de Janeiro and at Iguazu, while the Bolivian days explore lagoons, the Uyuni Salt Flat and the landmarks of La Paz. A separate wine tasting is available at an additional cost in Chile, which is also part of the wider itinerary. Here we explain what is actually included and how to choose a journey focused on food and wine without inflated expectations.
---

## Food and wine across three countries: where it fits into the actual itinerary

This selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with [Argentina](/argentina/), [Bolivia](/bolivia/) and [Brazil](/brazil/) among their main countries and the Food and Wine interest. At present, the selection includes the [20-day journey through six countries from Rio to Machu Picchu](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/). In addition to the three selected countries, it visits Uruguay, Chile and Peru.

The food-and-wine tag applies to **the itinerary as a whole**; it does not promise a wine tour in every country. The confirmed programme includes a tango dinner in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) with Argentine wines. In [Brazil](/brazil/), the focus is on Rio and Iguazu Falls, while [Bolivia](/bolivia/) is devoted to high-altitude scenery and archaeological sites. In these two sections, standalone tastings, winery visits and cooking classes are not listed as mandatory services.

This distinction matters when choosing a trip. The tour suits someone who wants to discover several countries and spend one memorable evening enjoying Argentine food. A systematic exploration of winemaking and cuisine in all three countries would require a customised itinerary, with the cities, timing and content of visits agreed separately.

## Argentina: dinner at a tango show in Buenos Aires

After the Brazilian part of the journey, travellers arrive in Buenos Aires. The city programme includes historic neighbourhoods, squares and an introduction to tango. One evening features a **tango show with dinner**: the description specifies a multi-course menu of traditional dishes and Argentine wines. Here, gastronomy is part of a particular cultural event rather than a tasting at a winery.

What makes such an evening appealing? It combines local cuisine with one of Argentina's best-known art forms. However, dinner during a show differs from a dedicated wine tour: the programme does not promise a trip to Mendoza, visits to wine cellars or a meeting with a winemaker.

If Argentine wine is your main interest, compare [food-and-wine trips in Argentina](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/) and decide in advance whether to add a separate wine-producing region. This would change the original itinerary's duration and logistics. It would be misleading to present an ordinary visit to Buenos Aires as a vineyard visit.

## Brazil: Rio and Iguazu rather than a pre-included culinary tour

The Brazilian section of the [20-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) begins in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/). The route introduces visitors to the city and its famous viewpoints before a flight to [Iguazu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). The programme describes the waterfall excursions in detail, including visits to the Brazilian and Argentine sides.

These days do not include a mandatory cooking workshop, a guided food-market visit or a tasting menu. So the visit to Brazil within this multi-day itinerary **is not equivalent to a dedicated culinary tour of Brazil**.

If food is one of your main reasons to travel, it makes more sense to discuss a specific stop in Rio and whether free time can be allocated to a chosen restaurant or culinary excursion. These experiences can be proposed as part of an individually agreed programme, but they must not be treated as prepaid or included by default. The distinction between a general itinerary and a themed product is clear in the [catalogue of food-and-wine trips in Brazil](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/brazil/).

## Bolivia: a high-altitude route and limitations on culinary stops

After the Chilean section, the group crosses Bolivia's high-altitude region. The itinerary describes colourful lagoons, desert landscapes, the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/), a flight to La Paz and the archaeological monuments of Tiwanaku. This part of the trip devotes substantial time to a four-wheel-drive route, Altiplano scenery and the history of an ancient culture.

A standalone culinary programme in Bolivia **is not advertised** in the available schedule. Ordinary meals during transfers should therefore not be presented as a professional tasting of Bolivian cuisine, a market visit with a food guide or a cooking masterclass.

There is also a practical reason to approach additions carefully: this section travels at considerable altitude and includes drives through remote areas. An extra restaurant evening or specialised excursion would need time and the right choice of city; it cannot simply be inserted between long driving days without revising the schedule. For this purpose, explore [other food-and-wine itineraries featuring Bolivia](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/bolivia/) and discuss separately which format is actually available on your travel dates.

## Where the wider journey offers a winery visit

An important detail lies **outside the selected three countries**. In [Santiago, Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/), an additional visit to wineries in the Maipo Valley with a tasting is offered. The description explicitly labels it an **excursion at an additional charge**.

This is the clearest winery experience offered on the 20-day itinerary, but it belongs to [Chile](/chile/), not Argentina, Bolivia or Brazil. It cannot automatically be counted among the prepaid services or presented as a wine programme in the three selected countries.

Travellers have two different options. The first is to keep the extensive six-country trip as it is, with the tango dinner in Argentina and the nature-focused programme elsewhere. The second is to arrange a winery day in Chile in advance and consider additional culinary stops wherever flights and available time permit. The second option requires confirmation of the price and availability of individual services.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_latin_america_six_countries_20_days_2026}}

## Why the three countries do not form a separate wine itinerary

The countries are grouped in the catalogue because **all three genuinely form part of one multi-day tour** tagged with the food-and-wine theme. However, the geographical journey is much broader: Brazil and Argentina come first, followed by Uruguay and Chile, then Bolivia and Peru. Sights, flights and mountain transfers occupy a substantial share of the days.

A trip dedicated to wine typically allocates time differently: time for each tasting, journeys between wineries, lunch on site and the opportunity to compare several producers. The current 20-day itinerary is designed to introduce travellers to Latin America; its culinary elements complement the principal natural and cultural experiences.

The choice therefore comes down to a simple question: **do you want one major tour with several culinary experiences, or a dedicated journey in which food shapes the entire route?** For the first option, the existing programme is suitable. For the second, explore [all multi-country food-and-wine itineraries](/multi-country/interests/food-and-wine/) and compare those with actual winery visits and tastings.

## How to arrange a journey with a culinary focus

If the tango dinner remains the main event, it needs to fit the city excursions and the actual time in Buenos Aires. If wine is the priority, select specific regions rather than relying only on a country's name in the catalogue. A winery visit needs time for both the transfer and the experience itself; adding one to a long tour may require changing that day's itinerary.

The Bolivian section is best planned with altitude, distances and travellers' well-being in mind. Meals, rest and acclimatisation are more important in practice than squeezing another themed activity into an already full schedule. The Rio and Iguazu days likewise need sufficient time for excursions; any cooking activity must fit the existing timetable.

We help compare the original programme with an individual version day by day, including countries, services included and additional expenses. Until a change is agreed, the only reliable list of services is the one specified for the chosen tour.

## Frequently asked questions about food and wine in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil

### Are wine tastings included in all three countries?

No. The confirmed culinary experience within the selected three countries is a tango-show dinner with Argentine wines in Buenos Aires. Mandatory winery visits in Brazil and Bolivia are not listed in the 20-day programme.

### Is the Maipo Valley winery excursion included?

No. This tasting is offered in Chile as an optional excursion at an additional charge. Chile is part of the complete six-country tour, but it is not in the selected Argentina–Bolivia–Brazil combination.

### Can this journey be turned into a full culinary tour?

A customised itinerary can be discussed, with specific visits added and time allocated to them. However, that would be a separately agreed version of the programme, not a set of activities already included in the existing tour.

### Is the six-country itinerary suitable for a first introduction to the region's cuisine?

Yes, if the main goal is an extensive journey through Latin America, with dinner in Buenos Aires and a possible wine excursion in Chile as additional experiences. For a trip primarily focused on wineries, choose a route in which visits to producers are part of the core programme.

lead: >-
  On nature-focused tours through Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil, the highlights are seeing Iguazu from both sides and then moving from humid forests to the lagoons and the Uyuni Salt Flat. The current itineraries also necessarily include Chile and Peru: consider the entire journey, especially the high-altitude section travelled by four-wheel-drive vehicles.
---

## Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil: where nature takes centre stage

Our selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. In every qualifying programme, natural attractions are spread across an extensive journey through **Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru**. Some journeys continue into other countries. The three countries named in this selection therefore belong to a larger trip, rather than a standalone tour limited strictly to them.

For experiencing nature, the order matters: the tropical and subtropical landscapes of [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) and [Iguazu Falls on the Brazilian side](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/), followed by trails at the same waterfalls in Argentina, and only after the Chilean section, the Bolivian highlands. Humidity, temperature, overnight altitude and transport conditions all change within a few days. When comparing itineraries, focus first on **time actually spent at natural attractions**, not the number of countries in the title.

## Brazil: Rio's urban mountains and panoramic views of Iguazu

In Rio, nature is constantly visible alongside the city: the bay, beaches and granite peaks form an instantly recognisable panorama. Programmes include trips up Corcovado and Sugarloaf Mountain; these are sightseeing excursions, not multi-day hikes through tropical rainforest. A longer exploration of forest ecosystems would require a separate itinerary.

The main nature day of the Brazilian section takes place near [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). Walkways on this side provide views of several cascades and the broad sweep of the falls at once. Remnants of the Atlantic Forest surround them. UNESCO recognises the Brazilian and Argentine national parks as adjoining protected areas of the same waterfall complex. The panoramic Brazilian viewpoint and the Argentine boardwalk walks complement one another.

Some itineraries offer **optional**, rather than automatically included, activities: a visit to the [Bird Park](/brazil/place/parque-das-aves/) and a boat ride near the falls. For a nature holiday with children or waterfall photography, discuss these separately, together with the excursion's duration and access conditions on the day of the visit.

## Argentina: getting closer to the water before changing the focus of the journey

On the [Puerto Iguazú](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/) side, walkways pass closer to individual streams and the [Devil's Throat](/argentina/place/garganta-del-diablo/) area. Allow time for walking, and take account of boardwalk conditions and the weather. High water levels may lead to temporary closures of individual sections. The waterfalls in the two countries are separate visits: seeing both sides takes time, transport and a border crossing.

After Iguazu, most of the itineraries considered here continue to [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). In the capital, the route is predominantly cultural, including a city tour, historic neighbourhoods and tango. This distinction matters if nature is your chief reason for travelling: **the Argentine nature experience here is concentrated at Iguazu**, rather than covering Patagonia, glaciers or the lake district.

## Bolivia: lagoons, geothermal fields and the Uyuni Salt Flat

The Bolivian nature section begins after [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) in Chile. According to the itinerary, travellers cross the border and board 4×4 vehicles. The road passes [Laguna Verde](/bolivia/place/laguna-verde/), the rocky landscapes of the Dalí Desert, thermal springs and the Sol de Mañana geysers before reaching [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/). James's flamingos are mentioned at the lagoon: their habitat is on the route, but an actual sighting depends on natural conditions.

The next section crosses other high-altitude lakes, volcanic landscapes and the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). In dry weather the salt surface resembles a vast pale plain; when there is water, it may mirror the clouds. **The mirror effect cannot be guaranteed for particular dates.** Ground moisture also affects vehicle routes and access to individual locations. After the four-wheel-drive section, the journey continues to [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/).

Prepare for dry air, wind, intense sunlight, cold evenings and considerable altitude. The difficulty comes less from the distance walked than from moving rapidly from lowlands to the Altiplano and spending long hours on the road.

## Which tours to choose for nature stops

| Programme | Distinguishing feature |
|---|---|
| [5 countries in 18 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) | Main group itinerary |
| [6 countries in 20 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) | Adds Uruguay |
| [8 countries in 32 days](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) | Continues to the Galápagos |
| [5 countries with the Champions' Parade](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) | Festive focus in Rio |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_5_stran_latinskoj_ameriki,tour_latin_america_six_countries_20_days_2026,tour_south_america_eight_countries_32_days_2026}}

These tours share similar natural stops in the five main countries, but differ in total length and additional cultural and festive events. The [32-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) includes a Galápagos section in Ecuador; **the Galápagos lie outside the three countries named in this selection's title**. If your main priority is the scenery of the Andes, Iguazu and Uyuni, a shorter itinerary may be more convenient.

For routes with particular emphasis on Peru's landscapes, see [Argentina, Bolivia and Peru: Nature](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_peru/interests/nature/). If the transition from Rio to Atacama appeals to you, see the [nature selection for Bolivia, Brazil and Chile](/multi-country/bolivia_brazil_chile/interests/nature/).

## Seasons, altitude and planning nature days

There is no single ideal season for both Iguazu and Uyuni. Heavy rain, heat and humidity are possible at the falls; nights on the Bolivian plateau can be very cold even during the warmer months. The rainy season may produce reflections on the salt flat but can also make driving more difficult. Choose the season to suit your priority attraction and discuss the compromises on the other sections in advance.

The US CDC's travel guidance on altitude recommends gradual ascent and acclimatisation. On this itinerary, the journey from [Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) to the high-altitude lagoons and the subsequent overnight stays in Bolivia are especially significant. Travellers with heart or lung conditions should discuss a high-altitude itinerary with a doctor in advance and check any altitude exclusions in their insurance. Ada Tours helps coordinate flights, overland sections, rest and preparation for changes in climate.

## Frequently asked questions about nature in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil

### Can I see both sides of Iguazu on one trip?

Yes. The itineraries considered include the Brazilian and Argentine sides of the falls on different days. The second visit involves crossing an international border.

### Will Uyuni look like a mirror?

It can, when a suitable layer of water covers the salt flat. Surface conditions depend on rainfall and the season, so this experience cannot be promised in advance.

### Are Chile and Peru included in the journey?

Yes. Every currently available tour in this particular selection also passes through Chile and Peru. A journey limited to the three named countries would require a separately planned individual itinerary.

## Iguazu and Bolivia's lagoons on the way to wildlife watching in the Galápagos

Our selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil are among the main countries, while the scheduled wildlife encounters may occur elsewhere on the complete journey. On the [eight-country South American tour](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/), such excursions are included in the Galápagos Islands in Ecuador. To compare scenic trips, including the [five-country Latin America group tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), see the [selection of nature itineraries through these three countries](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil/interests/nature/).

The Brazilian, Argentine and Bolivian sections feature two very different main natural settings. Humid forest and the waterfall complex on the Brazil–Argentina border give way to Bolivia's dry high-altitude deserts and salt lakes. Both regions are home to birds and other animals, but a visit to a waterfall or lagoon **is not the same as a dedicated wildlife safari**. Viewpoints and the journeys between them occupy much of the available time.

## Argentina and Brazil: two sides of one natural complex

On the Brazilian section, travellers fly to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and follow walkways offering broad panoramas of the cascades. The itinerary then crosses the border to see the Argentine side from [Puerto Iguazú](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). Trails here approach the water more closely, including the [Devil's Throat](/argentina/place/garganta-del-diablo/) area.

Both national parks protect sections of the Atlantic Forest. Its inhabitants include howler monkeys, tapirs and jaguars; this describes the ecosystem, **not a list of animals the excursion promises you will see**. What visitors can plan on along these routes is the landscape itself: waterfalls, humid forest, roaring water and viewing bridges. Heavy rain and high river levels occasionally restrict access to specific walkways, so check the conditions at the individual park before visiting.

The programmes offer the **optional** opportunity to visit the [Bird Park near Iguazu](/brazil/place/parque-das-aves/). This is a separate managed attraction with aviaries, and should not be confused with observing free-living birds in the forest. Macuco Safari, combining a forest excursion and a motorboat trip, is likewise listed as an optional activity rather than a mandatory part of every tour. If birds are your main priority, agree on this excursion and the time available for it first, and then choose the programme by price and duration.

## Bolivia: high-altitude lagoons and Uyuni landscapes

The Bolivian section begins after [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) in Chile. Four-wheel-drive vehicles cross the [Laguna Verde](/bolivia/place/laguna-verde/) area, geysers and thermal springs before reaching [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/). James's flamingos are mentioned in the description of this stop. That is information about the lagoon's inhabitants; a separate birdwatching activity is not specified for the day.

The next section includes more high-altitude lagoons, including [Hedionda](/bolivia/place/laguna-hedionda/), before the route reaches the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). Uyuni is primarily known for its salt landscape, not mass encounters with wildlife. Both days focus on natural scenery. A possible encounter with birds beside a lagoon should be distinguished from a dedicated wildlife-watching excursion.

Laguna Colorada lies at approximately 4,400 metres; conditions on the road between lagoons and geysers are significantly harsher than at Iguazu. The principle for observing wildlife here is straightforward: keep your distance, account for wind and cold, stay on permitted routes and do not approach feeding or nesting sites for a photograph. Flamingo numbers and behaviour depend on natural conditions, season and the state of the water bodies.

## How the three countries connect in the current itinerary

| Section | Main nature highlight |
|---|---|
| Brazil | Iguazu panoramas and humid forest |
| Argentina | Iguazu cascades and forest trails |
| Bolivia | Flamingos at lagoons and the salt flat |

The order of travel matters. The itinerary does not go directly “Argentina – Bolivia – Brazil”. After Iguazu and Buenos Aires, the journeys considered include a flight to Santiago, followed by Atacama, high-altitude Bolivia and Peru. The [three-country combination page](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil/) also shows itineraries without a particular nature interest; this selection instead focuses on which landscapes and wildlife encounters make the long transfers worthwhile.

On the [eight-country South American tour](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/), the Galápagos Islands belong to the Ecuador section. An included sea excursion follows one of two alternative routes: North Seymour and Bachas, or South Plaza and Cape Carrión. These introduce visitors to birds, sea lions and other island wildlife; the choice of route is confirmed after booking. This section of the complete journey is the basis for the Wildlife Watching interest. Also compare [multi-country wildlife-watching tours](/multi-country/interests/wildlife/) if you would prefer a different region.

## Climate, altitude and organising wildlife encounters

At Iguazu, expect humidity, spray and possible rain. Non-slip footwear and protection for documents and camera equipment against water are useful. Bolivia's highlands call for very different clothing: warm layers, wind protection and protection from intense sunshine. A single bag needs to accommodate light clothing for the subtropics and insulated clothing for the Altiplano.

Even more important than clothing is how you feel at altitude. Altitude sickness can develop during an ascent without acclimatisation, even in very fit travellers. The [five-country, 18-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) includes a stop in San Pedro de Atacama before the journey into Bolivia, but that does not guarantee the absence of symptoms. Compare the altitudes of overnight stays, discuss contraindications with a doctor and allow for a lighter schedule if you feel unwell.

Border crossings require documents that meet the requirements of **every country on the complete itinerary**, including Chile and Peru. Visa, transit and re-entry rules must be checked according to nationality and travel dates; a single rule cannot apply to all passengers. Also clarify national-park fees, optional excursions and the use of cash and cards in Bolivia's smaller communities. We help coordinate the travel sequence, overland border crossings and the activities selected, but sightings of a particular bird species and acceptance of a particular means of payment cannot be guaranteed.

## Which programmes to compare

On the [five-country group tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), nature days at Iguazu and the lagoons form part of a relatively busy itinerary. The [six-country journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) adds Montevideo. The [long eight-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) extends the nature experiences to Ecuador, but also adds flights and long transfers.

The table below compares programmes with included opportunities to watch wild animals or birds. Scenic trips without those activities can be compared in the [nature-travel selection](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil/interests/nature/). On a multi-country tour, wildlife watching may take place outside the countries in the selection title: always check the complete route and the individual days.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_south_america_eight_countries_32_days_2026}}

If you are interested in a single ecosystem, also compare [nature tours in Brazil](/interests/nature/tours/brazil/) and [nature tours in Bolivia](/interests/nature/tours/bolivia/). Combining the three countries makes sense when you genuinely want to experience the contrast between the Atlantic Forest and high-altitude lakes and can allow enough time for a complete cross-border itinerary.

## Frequently asked questions about nature in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil

### Are flamingos guaranteed at Laguna Colorada?

No. The routes visit flamingo habitat, but a dedicated birdwatching activity is not specified for the Bolivian day. Encounters depend on natural conditions, while the timing and restrictions at the stop depend on the actual itinerary.

### Is the Bird Park included in the price of every programme?

No. On the itineraries considered, the Bird Park near Iguazu is an optional activity. Confirm whether it is included in your chosen tour before paying.

### Can I see both sides of Iguazu on the same journey?

Yes. The current itineraries described include both the Brazilian and Argentine sides. The order and accessible trails depend on the schedule, weather and park rules.

### Is there a separate tour covering exactly these three countries?

The programmes listed also include other main countries. To arrange a trip limited to Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil, the itinerary, flights and duration would need to be planned separately.

## Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile: how the journey works

**The main route follows Brazil → Argentina → Chile → Bolivia, then Peru.** It begins with [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), the Brazilian and Argentine sides of Iguazu Falls, and [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). Travellers then fly to [Santiago, Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/), continue to [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) and cross Bolivia's highlands towards [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) and [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/).

The catalogue title means that **all four selected countries are part of the main itinerary**; it does not limit the journey to those countries. Every current programme also visits [Peru](/peru/), including [Lake Titicaca near Puno](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and [Lima](/peru/place/lima/). Our catalogue contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Compare the number of days, festival schedules and actual services included rather than relying on the promise of “four countries”.

| Section | What to check |
|---|---|
| Rio and Iguazu | Days and border crossings |
| Buenos Aires | Connecting airport |
| Atacama → Bolivia | Altitude and four-wheel-drive transport |
| Peru | Entry to Machu Picchu |

For choosing the order of countries yourself, see our [main multi-country travel section](/multi-country/). This selection addresses a more specific question: how to combine Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile on one confirmed Ada Tours itinerary.

## Iguazu: two national parks and a border-crossing day

On the Brazilian side, the journey passes through [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). To see the Argentine section of the falls, you need to cross the border and reach [Puerto Iguazú](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). This is a separate international transfer, not a walk between neighbouring viewpoints. Border formalities, road conditions and admission to each park affect the length of the day.

The airport serving Foz do Iguaçu is **IGU**, while Argentine Puerto Iguazú uses **IGR**. A ticket departing from one airport cannot be used at the other. Next comes [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), where it is also essential to distinguish **EZE**, the international Ezeiza Airport, from **AEP**, the city airport Aeroparque. If an airport change is necessary, allow time for baggage collection, the road transfer and check-in again.

On the current five-country itineraries, sightseeing on the Argentine side is sometimes combined with a flight to Buenos Aires. With that schedule, the time actually available for trails and viewpoints matters more than a generic promise to “visit Iguazu”. Check the programme for the specific day and whether the necessary transfer is included.

## Chile and Bolivia: why the main challenge begins after Santiago

After [Santiago](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/), the programmes continue to Calama and [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/). The urban pace then gives way to four-wheel-drive journeys across the Bolivian plateau. Main natural stops include [Laguna Verde](/bolivia/place/laguna-verde/), [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/), geyser fields and the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/).

**The altitude of your overnight stops and how quickly you ascend matter more here than your usual fitness level.** According to the CDC Yellow Book, altitude illness can affect healthy, fit people; the body needs time to acclimatise. For a route involving a rapid ascent from low elevations to the Andes, discuss altitude tolerance and insurance terms with your doctor in advance. On travel days, pay attention to sleep, rest, how you feel and whether the exertion can be adjusted.

Read the detailed itinerary literally: where the four-wheel-drive section begins, where overnight stays are scheduled, how many hours the roads take and whether there are substantial breaks. Natural attractions in Bolivia are far apart. The lagoons and salt flat form an intensive part of the journey, where comfort depends on transport arrangements, weather and road accessibility.

At [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/), the water-mirror effect is not guaranteed on any particular day. Reflections appear under suitable conditions after rainfall; the dry salt flat looks different. When selecting a season, remember that rain also affects access to certain areas. An ideal mirror photograph online is not a weather guarantee for your travel dates.

## Entry and documents: requirements for five countries

Start by listing every country you will **actually enter**, including Peru and any transit countries on international tickets. Requirements can differ according to nationality, passport type, purpose of travel and the need to re-enter. Checking only the first country of arrival is not enough.

For holders of ordinary Russian passports, the Brazilian embassy confirms short-term visa-free entry for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Requirements for Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru must each be checked before departure. Chile has a temporary-stay category called *Permanencia Transitoria*, and certain nationalities need advance consular authorisation. Peru's migration service notes a minimum passport validity of **six months** upon entry.

On every entry into Chile, travellers complete the **SAG** declaration concerning plant and animal products, including items in ordinary luggage. Food, seeds and some souvenirs may need to be declared; an inspector makes the final admission decision. The overland section between Atacama and Bolivia is subject to this border requirement just like arrival at a Chilean airport.

For Argentina, travellers should have medical insurance: a declaration concerning its possession is enshrined in immigration law. When choosing a policy, check coverage specifically for high-altitude travel and excursions. Standard insurance may exclude activities at certain elevations.

## Five currencies and spending between cities

The route uses **BRL** (Brazilian real), **ARS** (Argentine peso), **CLP** (Chilean peso), **BOB** (Boliviano) and **PEN** (Peruvian sol). The two currencies called “peso” belong to different countries. Before exchanging money, separate expenses included in the tour from those you will pay independently.

A bank card is convenient in many cities, but local cash is sensible in smaller communities and high-altitude areas. Paying directly in US dollar notes is not universally accepted. ATMs, fees and exchange rates vary by country and city. Russian-issued Visa and Mastercard cards do not work on international networks; for a card issued by a foreign bank, check country restrictions and limits.

The programme price depends on the services provided. Some packages include domestic flights and transfers, while others charge separately for optional excursions, some meals or guiding in a particular language. For example, current Ada Tours itineraries include sections with Russian-speaking and English-speaking guides. Do not assume that the services included in one programme apply to the others.

## Weather in the tropics and Andes: what to pack

The first days in [Rio](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) call for clothes suited to warm, humid weather. At [Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), protection against spray is useful. In [Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) and on Bolivia's plateau, pack warm layers for mornings and evenings, a windproof jacket, sun protection and shoes suitable for uneven ground. It can be cold at altitude even when Santiago is warm.

Layered clothing and a small daypack are a practical combination. Check baggage weight restrictions separately before domestic flights. A large suitcase that works well for a week on the coast becomes less convenient during successive flights and four-wheel-drive transfers.

Southern Hemisphere summer holiday periods suit the dates of some event-based tours, but they do not guarantee identical conditions in every region. If the objective is Carnival or New Year in Rio, that event fixes the start of the itinerary and the other nature sections must be organised around it.

## Four current programmes: how they differ

All four tours cover **five countries**, although their events, duration and format differ.

- [“5 Latin American countries in 18 days”](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) is a group itinerary through Rio, Iguazu, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Atacama, Uyuni, Titicaca and Machu Picchu.
- [“Highlights of 5 countries in 19 days”](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-carnival-private-tour/) is a private format with a Carnival event in Rio; the exact festive activities and included services are specified in its programme.
- [The 19-day New Year tour across five countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-new-year-group-tour-19-days/) is a group journey celebrating New Year on Copacabana and then visiting all five countries.
- [“5 countries with the Carnival Champions' Parade” in 18 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) is a group programme including the Champions' Parade and a transfer to the Sambadrome under the stated terms.

If [Bolivia](/bolivia/) and high-altitude landscapes attract you most, compare the length of the section from Atacama to La Paz. If Rio and cultural events are your priority, focus on the festive dates and the Sambadrome programme. Check tickets, transfers, meals and guiding language included in the specific tour package, particularly when deciding between group and private formats.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I buy a trip to only the four countries, without Peru?

Every current ready-made offer on this page also includes Peru. Changing the itinerary must be discussed separately: removing the Peruvian section affects flights, overnight stays and the order of excursions. It is not an existing standard option on every tour.

### How difficult is the route through Bolivia?

The main factors are altitude, the duration of overland transfers and the weather. Preparing for altitude matters even for physically fit travellers. Before booking, review the overnight stops and the days following the Chile–Bolivia border crossing.

### Is one day enough for both sides of Iguazu?

That depends on the schedule, border queues and the time available in the parks. Both sides are included in the five-country itineraries, but the pace of each day differs. For a relaxed visit, assess the actual timetable rather than just a list of sights.

### Do I need cash in all the countries?

Some expenses may already be included in the tour price, so large advance holdings of every currency are unnecessary. For small payments and remote areas, some local cash and a backup payment method are useful.

### How long does such a journey take?

The programmes presented last 18–19 days and also cover Peru. The actual amount of free time depends on the number of flights and overland transfers, so two itineraries of the same length can feel very different.

## Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile: where the adventure begins

[Argentina](/argentina/), [Bolivia](/bolivia/), [Brazil](/brazil/) and [Chile](/chile/) make it possible to travel in one journey from humid forests at Iguazu to the dry high-altitude plateaus of the Andes. It is the contrast in conditions that shapes the experience: travellers explore cities in Rio and Buenos Aires, follow park walkways at Iguazu, prepare for altitude in Atacama and change to four-wheel-drive vehicles on the Bolivian side.

Our themed selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with these four main countries and a substantial adventure component. **Filtering by four countries does not mean that the journey visits only those countries.** For example, the [18-day group itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) also includes Peru, while the [20-day journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) visits Uruguay too. Longer programmes continue to further destinations in South America.

It is therefore best to compare these trips day by day. On one itinerary, the main event is Rio's Carnival Champions' Parade; on another, New Year's Eve on Copacabana Beach. The high-altitude sections may nonetheless be very similar. [All tours through these four countries](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil_chile/) are listed separately from [multi-country adventure programmes](/multi-country/interests/adventure/).

## Brazil: from Rio to Iguazu Falls

Many itineraries start in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/). Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain, city walks and the Atlantic coast fill several days before the active section in the Andes. Travellers then fly to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/), where forest walkways and viewing platforms follow the waterfalls.

Iguazu impresses with the roar and power of its cascades, but **a regular visit to the national park remains a sightseeing walk**, not an extreme rafting expedition. The [18-day group tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) also offers Macuco Safari, combining a section through the forest with a motorboat ride near the falls. The programme lists it as a separately paid option. If the boat excursion matters to you, confirm its availability and conditions before making your final choice.

A trip to Brazil does not automatically involve a jungle trek or rafting. These days are designed for Rio and Iguazu, while the possibility of adding a more active experience depends on the particular programme and the free time available.

## Argentina: the other side of Iguazu and on to Buenos Aires

On the [Argentine side of Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), walking trails approach the water and individual cascades more closely. This feels different from the broad panoramas on the Brazilian side. On the 18-day itinerary, a transfer to the airport and a flight to [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) follow the Argentine park visit.

Allow sufficient time to see both sides, including the border crossing. The distance between parks on a map is deceptive: the journey involves transfers, document checks and separate entrance areas. High water levels can also close some trails temporarily.

Buenos Aires adds culture and city walks to the journey. Some itineraries include a tango show. **The Argentine section of these programmes should not automatically be described as trekking or a mountain expedition.** The principal extended adventure segment comes later, after Chile, when travellers cross the Andes into Bolivia.

## Chile: San Pedro de Atacama before the high-altitude route

After Santiago, the route continues to Calama and then [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/). On the [18-day group tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), this day is partly intended for acclimatisation before the journey to Uyuni. The desert plains, volcanic peaks and dry air differ sharply from Brazil and Argentina.

This is a nature-focused section in its own right, although much of the time is spent flying, transferring and preparing for altitude. Some programmes offer an optional evening astronomy excursion. Whether it is possible depends on the individual tour's conditions and the weather; it is not included as standard in every trip.

**The most demanding part of the route is still ahead**, so before entering Bolivia it is useful to consider how you feel and where the overnight stays are arranged. Good physical fitness is no guarantee against altitude sickness. Travellers with conditions affected by altitude should discuss the route with a doctor in advance. The schedule should not be rushed simply to fit in another desert stop.

## Bolivia: four-wheel-drive vehicles, lagoons and the Uyuni Salt Flat

The Bolivian section is the clearest adventure portion of the itinerary. After crossing the border, travellers take 4×4 vehicles towards [Laguna Verde](/bolivia/place/laguna-verde/), passing the rock formations of the Salvador Dalí Desert, the Polques thermal springs and the Sol de Mañana geysers. The day ends at [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/), known for its reddish water and James's flamingos.

This is a high-altitude region, not an ordinary car excursion around a capital city. On the [18-day programme](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), Laguna Colorada is described at an altitude of around 4,400 metres, with an overnight stay in simple conditions on the desert plateau. Long driving sections, temperature changes and limited comfort shape the demands of the trip as much as the number of scenic stops.

The following day passes the Honda, Chiar Khota, Hedionda and Cañapa lagoons, Ollagüe volcano and the Chiguana Salt Flat on the way to [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). The programme names Colchani, the “Eyes of Water” and Incahuasi Island with its cacti. In the dry season travellers see a white salt surface, while in the rainy season parts may be covered by water. **A mirror-like surface is not guaranteed on every date**, nor is access to every section of the salt flat during heavy rains.

It is important to understand the travel format: a 4×4 off-road excursion involves substantial time in a vehicle and stops at natural attractions. It is not a technical volcano ascent or a multi-day trek on foot. Mountaineering, demanding trekking and dedicated expeditions require different confirmed products and arrangements.

## Preparing for a journey through the Andes

The climate changes repeatedly along this itinerary: humid Rio, the Iguazu Falls region, urban Buenos Aires, dry Atacama and Bolivia's high-altitude plateau. Pack light clothes for warm areas, warm layers for high elevations, sun protection and comfortable walking shoes. For the off-road section, clarify the permitted luggage weight, driving time, frequency of stops and accommodation type in advance.

Altitude deserves separate planning. Moving abruptly to lagoons above 4,000 metres can bring on symptoms of altitude sickness. **Agreeing on the pace, overnight stops and medical limitations is particularly important on this section.** The waterfalls, city excursions and Bolivian high-altitude journey should not be assumed to require the same preparation.

The itinerary crosses international borders and includes flights. Check entry and transit requirements for every traveller's nationality, baggage conditions, necessary tickets and payment arrangements for optional excursions. The crossing from Chile to Bolivia is planned separately, followed in some programmes by the onward journey to Peru.

Ada Tours helps put flights and transfers into a coherent sequence and align the programme with the actual length of your holiday. If nature is your main priority, preserving enough days for Atacama and Uyuni is more sensible than adding numerous new stops to an already full itinerary.

## Frequently asked questions about adventures in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile

### Where is the main off-road section?

In Bolivia, after travelling from Chilean Atacama. On the [18-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), the 4×4 route passes lagoons and geysers on its way to the Uyuni Salt Flat.

### Is Macuco Safari included in the Iguazu programme?

On the 18-day group itinerary, it is listed as an additional paid excursion. A regular waterfall visit is included separately.

### Is mountaineering experience required for a trip to Uyuni?

The published programme describes an off-road journey rather than a technical climb. However, the altitude, long drives and basic overnight conditions require preparation and an assessment of your health.

### Does the selection include Peru?

Yes. Some current itineraries continue from Bolivia into Peru, past Titicaca towards Cusco and Machu Picchu. Filtering by Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile means those four countries are included, not that others are excluded.

### Can I see a mirror-like salt-flat surface in any season?

No. Surface conditions depend on rainfall and road access. Match your chosen dates to the appearance you hope to see and the accessibility of the route.

### How do the Carnival and standard options differ?

The [Champions' Parade tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) specifically includes attendance at the festive event in Rio. The [standard 18-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) has broadly similar geographic stops, but a different event programme and different travel conditions.
